items.title: Fed policymakers at odds over causes of high inflation By Reuters
items.excerpt: WASHINGTON, Nov 25 (Reuters) - US inflation likely jumped again in October, and data due on Wednesday will be key for Federal Reserve officials debating whether to raise interest rates next month and how to frame the likely rate path into next year. But no one should expect quick agreement. Fed policymakers and staff remain divided over whether inflation is being driven by overheating demand or by supply shocks that are likely to fade, and even over whether the source of inflation matters, with their credibility on the line after a nearly six-year inflation overshoot. The argument has been festering since President Donald Trump returned to the White House in January 2025. Markets are poised for rate increases, perhaps as many as three in quick succession amid persistent inflation. But some analysts, and particularly members of the Trump administration, call the prospect of such a move by the Fed a mistake waiting to happen. ... The current inflation "shocks" are deliberate policy choices by Trump, first to impose steep tariffs last year and then to launch a war against Iran this year, a conflict that is still constraining oil shipments. The resulting change in inflation has been clear to Fed officials, who aim to maintain inflation at a 2% annual rate. The inflation flowing from the COVID-19 pandemic peaked in June 2022 but had subsided sufficiently toward 2% by September ... Then, shortly after returning to the White House, Trump began imposing tariffs that threatened to boost import prices by 30% or more — rates that were later tempered but are still seen as substantial. The US-Israeli war with Iran, launched in February, added more pressure as global oil prices surged 50% to about $120 a barrel. Inflation increased. Economists expect the Personal Consumption Expenditures Price Index, which the Fed uses for its target, to hit 3.8% in October versus 2.3% in March 2025. Core PCE, which excludes food and energy costs and is considered a better signal of trend inflation, is expected to be 3.2% in October versus 2.6% in March 2025. Conventional wisdom holds that central bankers need not be concerned about price increases stemming from tariffs. Importers might make one-time adjustments, with no change in the underlying inflation trend. Similarly, oil and other commodity prices often fluctuate wildly, but their ups and downs tend to even out. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and others contend that this set of circumstances is unfolding now and argue that the Fed should not raise rates to chase inflation that is likely to abate before long. The Fed "has fallen into the trap of making backward-looking policy," Robin Brooks, a senior fellow at the Brookings Institution, wrote recently. Brooks noted that oil prices, which were near $120 a barrel in October and will feed into Wednesday’s inflation reading, have fallen below $90 a barrel following the US midterm elections that changed control of Congress and led Trump to downplay further strikes against Iran. "The idea that inflation isn’t coming down fast enough ... is a bit silly, given all the supply shocks," Brooks wrote. Fed staff have reached a similar conclusion. "Total inflation was expected to step down sharply next year as energy prices decelerated," staff told policymakers last month in an economic outlook that anticipated inflation returning close to target in 2028, the minutes of the central bank’s October 27-28 policy meeting showed. An analysis by St. Louis Fed staff estimated that about two-thirds of "excess" core PCE inflation and 90% of "excess" headline inflation were due to supply shocks. ... An increasing number of policymakers, however, regard supply-shock effects as less relevant than the fact that inflation has not been improving and seems to be in the process of becoming more broadly rooted. Recent strong inflation and jobs data, coupled with healthy consumer spending, bullish economic growth and booming investment in artificial intelligence, have prompted markets to price in three more rate hikes. Together with the rate hike delivered in September, that monetary tightening would retrace the three cuts from 2025 and go a quarter of a percentage point higher. "Fed communications continued to lean in a hawkish direction ... with the debate increasingly centered on the pace, size and total magnitude of additional tightening rather than whether further rate increases are needed," Deutsche Bank economists wrote this week, noting the hiking bias in the October meeting minutes. "Officials broadly viewed inflation risks as elevated amid resilient demand, accommodative financial conditions (at least prior to the recent stock market selloff), and the potential for AI investment to outstrip capacity." Fed staff, while expecting price pressures to ease, noted that years of high inflation had made rising inflation expectations a "salient" risk. ... Although his staff concluded that inflation is largely supply-driven, St. Louis Fed President Alberto Musalem said he still sees demand playing a significant role, citing the economy growing above trend and the likelihood that "inflation persists meaningfully above 2%, absent further removal of monetary policy accommodation." He said several hikes are likely required.

items.title: Bessent faces a debt limit reckoning with Democrats - POLITICO
items.excerpt: Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has spent nearly two years publicly belittling Democratic lawmakers. Soon, he’ll need their help to keep the United States from descending into a fiscal crisis. The U.S. is on track to hit its $41.1 trillion borrowing limit within weeks of Democrats taking control of Congress, setting up a showdown that could come to a head as early as next summer. ... Bessent’s history of personal attacks will test whether he can broker a deal between President Donald Trump and Democratic leaders before Treasury runs out of cash to pay the nation’s bills. A protracted debt limit standoff, even if it ultimately gets resolved, could rattle bond markets and push up borrowing costs.

items.title: House Dems demand clarity on Homeland Security tech contracts - POLITICO
items.excerpt: More than two dozen Democrats are demanding answers from companies that supply the Department of Homeland Security with technology, including AI tools, about how the agency uses their products. The letter, shared exclusively with POLITICO, went to a dozen executives, including those at Palantir Technologies, Flock Safety and Clearview AI. The companies’ tools are used for purposes including immigration policing and border enforcement. The lawmakers are concerned that DHS is using the companies’ technologies to track and target immigrants and other marginalized communities. They also worry these services are being used to collect and analyze data about the broader U.S. population engaged in First Amendment-protected activity. “Your company’s engagement with DHS risks enabling a much broader surveillance apparatus that increasingly treats entire communities as data points to be monitored, analyzed, and controlled for profit and political power,” the missive states.

items.title: Trump puts contractors in the crossfire of coming Democratic probes
items.excerpt: The White House is ratcheting up its fight against investigations from Democrats coming into power in January, trying to head off their contact with government contractors who otherwise might cooperate with their probes. In an executive order issued late Friday, the administration seeks to cut off an avenue for Democrats to get information on its activities, requiring contractors to alert the White House and get its blessing before complying with any investigative demands. Contractors are widely used throughout government and have also been involved in a number of controversial projects spearheaded by Trump, like his renovation of the reflecting pool and the construction of a new ballroom in place of the demolished East Wing. While Democrats argue the order is unlawful, it could still have a chilling effect. Trump has threatened to pull funding from contractors who cooperate with the congressional probes. Rep. Dan Goldman (D-N.Y.), a former federal prosecutor, said while the premise of the order is “comical,” a pledge to cancel contracts “will make any business pause.” ... White House counsel Will Scharf has already penned two letters to congressional Democrats to signal resistance to their probes.

items.title: Trump and Newsom clash over death row commutations amid 2028 ambitions
items.excerpt: President Trump’s public rebuke of California Gov. Gavin Newsom’s (D) move to commute the sentences of California’s death row inmates is platforming the Golden State governor as a GOP foe while he mulls a presidential bid. Trump vowed to work to overturn the commutations and took a number of personal jabs at the governor while speaking at the Justice Department on Monday. While Trump is seeking to create a contrast with Newsom, the move could also inadvertently bolster the California governor as Democrats seek to turn the page on the Trump administration in 2028. ... Newsom announced earlier this month he will commute all 548 death sentences in the state, drawing praise from anti-death penalty advocates and backlash from prosecutors and victims’ family members.

items.title: John Travolta Celebrates Fans at Torino Prize Ceremony
items.excerpt: Honored with a lifetime achievement tribute at the Torino Film Festival, John Travolta chose to share the spotlight with a special someone: You. “Thank you for giving me the most beautiful career,” he said, his voice trembling with emotion as he dedicated the festival prize to his audience. “For the last 50 years, I’ve been able to explore and give audiences so many different characters. You’ve offered me the opportunity to sing, to dance and to play characters I would never have dreamed of.” “So, big thanks to you for letting me do what Shakespeare asks of us: to be, or not to be,” Travolta continued. “You allowed me to be. You never clipped my wings. You allowed me to fly so beautifully, on the screen and in the air.” Flanked by artistic director Giulio Base and director Roland Joffé, the American star was on-hand to kick off this year’s Torino Film Festival with the international premiere of Joffé’s “ November 1963,” which casts Travolta as a Chicago mafioso intimately involved in the JFK assassination. The actor-turned-filmmaker will also stick around to present his directorial debut “Propeller One-Way Night Coach,” which now lands in Turin after launching in Cannes.
